opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is something I've thought about a lot, because there was a wave of papers after the original lottery ticket work, things like SNIP, GraSP, and SynFlow, all claiming to find these sparse trainable subnetworks at initialization or very early in training. That's the dream, right? If you could find the ticket up front, you'd get the efficiency benefits for the whole training run.

For me the bar is pretty simple, and it's twofold. First, does the subnetwork actually match the accuracy of the full dense network, at a meaningful sparsity, when trained in isolation? And second, does it do better than the obvious baselines? The baselines matter enormously. The comparison I care about is magnitude pruning after training, or lottery ticket rewinding to an early point in training. Those set the ceiling for what's achievable. If you're well below that, you haven't really found a lottery ticket. You've found a sparse network that trains okay.

What really clarified things for us was a set of sanity checks. Take the mask a method produces and randomly shuffle which weights are pruned within each layer, keeping the per-layer sparsity the same. Or keep the mask but reinitialize the weights. If the method were truly identifying specific important weights, those ablations should hurt. For lottery tickets found through rewinding, they do hurt, a lot. But for the methods that prune at initialization, accuracy basically didn't change, and sometimes even improved. In some cases you could invert the scores and prune the weights the method thought were most important, and it was fine.

That tells you these methods aren't finding particular weights. They're essentially finding good layer-wise sparsity ratios. That's still useful, but it's a very different claim from "we found the lottery ticket at initialization." So my standard is that a method has to pass those ablations and close the gap to rewinding. And honestly, to my knowledge, nobody has convincingly done that at scale yet. The evidence keeps pointing to the idea that you need at least a little bit of training before the network becomes stable enough for the ticket to exist. Which, to me, is the more interesting scientific question anyway: what is happening in those early iterations that makes the ticket findable?

r001.rationale: It compares early-found subnetworks with post hoc magnitude pruning and lottery ticket rewinding, describing those as benchmarks for achievable quality.

r002.rationale: It says initialization-pruning methods performed about the same with shuffled masks or reinitialized weights, indicating they did not outperform those simple baselines.

r003.rationale: It says pruning the weights a method scored as most important was still fine, which undercuts the claim that the scores identify specific important weights.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about a lot, because the lottery ticket hypothesis is really a claim about what's possible, and then there's a separate question of whether any particular method actually gets you there. And I think those two things get conflated constantly.

The way I think about it is that you have to be really disciplined about baselines. When someone says "we found a sparse subnetwork at initialization, or very early in training, and it trains to full accuracy," the first thing I want to know is: compared to what? Because it turns out there are some very dumb baselines that do surprisingly well. If you take a random subnetwork at the same sparsity and train it, how does that do? If you take a subnetwork where you just keep the magnitude of the weights but shuffle which ones you keep within each layer, how does that do? And what we found, in the work I did with my collaborators looking at methods like SNIP and GraSP and SynFlow, was that a lot of these methods were essentially discovering a per-layer sparsity allocation. They were figuring out how many weights to keep in each layer, and once you controlled for that, the specific weights they chose didn't matter much. You could shuffle them and get the same accuracy. That's a really important finding, because it tells you the method isn't finding a lottery ticket in the sense we meant it. It's finding a good layer-wise budget, which is useful, but it's a different thing.

The second thing is you have to compare against what you actually get from training. Iterative magnitude pruning with rewinding, where you train the network, prune it, rewind to an early iteration, and retrain, is expensive, but it's the thing that empirically works at scale. So if your early-training method matches that at the same sparsity, great, you've genuinely done something. If it's far below that, then you've made a tradeoff, and that tradeoff should be stated clearly. It's fine to say "we're cheaper and we get eighty percent of the way there," but that's not the same as saying you found the ticket.

And then the third thing, which I think is underappreciated, is scale and setting. A lot of these results look wonderful on small networks on MNIST or CIFAR, and then when you go to a ResNet-50 on ImageNet they fall apart, or you have to change the method in ways that weren't advertised. We saw this with our own early lottery ticket results. At initialization it worked for small networks, and for larger networks you had to rewind to a point slightly into training, not all the way back. That was a real limitation and we tried to be upfront about it. So when I'm judging a new method, I want to see it on the hard setting, not just the convenient one.

I'd also add, honestly, a bit of healthy skepticism about the framing. There's a tendency in this area for the story to be more compelling than the evidence. "You can skip training and just find the winning ticket" is a beautiful narrative. But the honest state of things, as I understand it, is that the information that identifies a good sparse subnetwork emerges during training. It's not sitting there at initialization waiting to be read off by a clever scoring function. Early in training, yes, we can find it after a small fraction of the way through. At step zero, we haven't seen a method that convincingly does it on a nontrivial problem. So if someone claims otherwise, the burden of proof is on them, and the shuffling and reinitialization ablations are the first place I'd look.

r001.rationale: The response says early methods should be compared at the same sparsity against iterative magnitude pruning with rewinding, which it describes as the method that empirically works at scale.

r002.rationale: It says random subnetworks and subnetworks with selected weights shuffled within layers can achieve the same accuracy, showing that several early methods did no better than naive baselines once layer-wise sparsity was controlled.

r003.rationale: The response discusses shuffling selected weights while preserving layer-wise sparsity or magnitude, but does not describe reversing a method’s pruning rule and observing unchanged performance.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: what are you claiming to have found? If the claim is that you’ve found a lottery ticket early in training, then you should be able to take that subnetwork, train it from the point you identified, and get performance comparable to the original network. And you need to compare against a randomly chosen subnetwork of the same size. Otherwise, maybe you’ve just shown that a smaller network works well on that problem.

The other question is whether you’ve actually saved anything. How much computation went into finding that subnetwork? Did you need to train a dense network first, or run an expensive search? You can have a scientifically interesting result about which connections matter without having a practical way to make training cheaper. I’d want to evaluate those claims separately.

r001.rationale: The response recommends comparing an early-found subnetwork with the original network and a random subnetwork of the same size. It does not propose comparison with subnetworks found post hoc using lottery ticket methods.

r002.rationale: The response says a random same-size subnetwork is needed as a baseline, but does not state that purported early-ticket methods performed no better than naive baselines.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss reversing a pruning rule or unchanged performance under that reversal.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is: what are you comparing against? If you identify a sparse network early in training, and it trains well, that alone doesn’t tell you that you’ve found a lottery ticket. Maybe a randomly chosen network with the same sparsity would train just as well.

So I’d want to compare it against a random mask, and I’d also want to take the mask you found and randomly reinitialize the weights. Does keeping those particular initial weights actually help? And you have to account for the training you used to find the ticket. If the goal is to save computation, that work counts too.

Those are slightly different claims: finding a good sparse architecture, finding a particular initialization that matters, and finding a cheaper way to train. I’d judge success by which claim the method is making and whether the experiments really isolate it.

r001.rationale: It proposes comparisons with a random mask and reinitialized weights, but does not compare early-found subnetworks with subnetworks found post hoc using lottery ticket methods.

r002.rationale: It raises the possibility that a random mask might perform just as well, but does not state that purported early lottery ticket methods actually performed no better than naive baselines.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss reversing a pruning rule or unchanged performance under that reversal.
